title: sleep
hook: a sage wakes two sleeping princes by a river, and his words become a temple's dawn song
tomorrow: the breath again — every claim checked

segments.voice: Yesterday, sleep that isn't rest: Kumbhakarna woken by drums and elephants, and the honest words he spoke awake. What did you wake up to, and what was the first step? Day one thousand three hundred twenty.

Before sunrise, by a river, two young princes are asleep on the ground. The sage who is leading them, Vishvamitra, leans over and speaks. In paraphrase: Rama, fortunate son of Kausalya, the eastern dawn is breaking. Rise, tiger among men; the day's rites are waiting. It's a small moment early in Valmiki's Ramayana, a teacher waking his students. But those words didn't stay by the river. They became the opening of a hymn sung before dawn to wake the deity. Today, the last of the sleep days: the temple's night and morning.
screen: `TWO PRINCES ASLEEP BY A RIVER.` → `RAMA, THE DAWN IS BREAKING.` → `A HYMN TO WAKE GOD.`

segments.voice: The hymn is the Venkatesa Suprabhatam, sung at dawn at the Venkateswara temple at Tirumala. Suprabhatam means a good dawn. It opens with Vishvamitra's verse, and then turns to the Lord of the hill and asks him, verse after verse, to wake. At the other end of the day, some temples have a bedtime rite. The deity is laid to rest, the lamps are lowered, a last song is sung, and the doors are shut until morning. A few things to see in it. First, tradition speaks of these rites as care, not as a claim that God gets tired: the way a beloved member of the household is served. A day with God in it begins with a gentle waking and ends with a gentle night. Second, the waking is spoken. Vishvamitra doesn't shake the princes. He tells them the dawn is here and the day has work in it. A good waking names what's waiting. Third, the two ends of the day frame everything between. Look back over our days on sleep. Charaka counted sleep among the three supports of life. Uddalaka's bird settled at its tether, the mind at rest in the breath. Yajnavalkya's dreamer was self-lit, making chariots and rivers. His falcon folded its wings, and every daytime name was set down. The Yoga Sutras read the morning report: I slept well. Kumbhakarna woke up honest. And here, the night and the dawn held as worship. Tomorrow, the breath, which has been quietly running under all of it.
screen: `SUPRABHATAM: A GOOD DAWN` · `A BEDTIME RITE IN THE TEMPLE` · `CARE, NOT A CLAIM OF TIREDNESS` · `THE TWO ENDS FRAME THE DAY`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: frame the day. Sit comfortably and let the breath settle. Bring to mind the last moment before sleep tonight. Where will you be? What's the last thing you'll see? Let it be gentle, in your mind's eye: a lamp lowered, a door shut. Then the first moment of tomorrow. How would you like to be woken? Not shaken. Spoken to. Let one kind sentence come for that moment. Then rest between the two, breathing. If you pray, you can offer the night and the morning both. The bell holds the time.
Sleep. A support of life, a homecoming, a self-lit dream, a falcon's nest, a movement of the mind, a giant's waking, and a temple's night and dawn. Today's word.
Your line: sleep. Tonight, end the day with one gentle act; tomorrow, wake yourself or someone else with words instead of a jolt. Day one thousand three hundred twenty.
